110.t: Milhaud's class and the birth of the octet
110.s: Milhaud invites jazz players to write counterpoint for jazz instrumentation, which becomes the octet with Paul Desmond and Cal Tjader.
110.q: [ ] class, the octet was born, when he said, “How many of you in this class play jazz?” Five of us raised our hands. We thought that was going to be the end of – like any other conservatory. He said, “I’d like you to write your counterpoint and your compositions for jazz instrumentation, if you…

110.t: Forming the octet and its few gigs
110.s: The octet formed in Milhaud's class and played only a handful of concerts; his father called it the damndest noise.
110.q: Yeah. And once in a while, somebody will say, “Oh, but I heard you at University of California, Berkeley.” It’s a gig I forgot. So maybe there were four or five. But there weren’t many. At Mills College, Marines Memorial in San Francisco, College of Pacific in Stockton, University of California,…

136.t: Sitting in with Max Roach, Clifford Brown and Richie Powell
136.s: Joey Master subbed, Max played fast, and she recalls Clifford Brown's appearance and Richie Powell.
136.ch: Boston, Berklee and New York encounters
136.q: And Max Roach was … he always played, firstly, always incredibly fast. That was his style. So, first day, it was the second day? The pianist disappeared or something. So there was a pianist living in Boston, called Joey Master, he was noted, I guess, so he was subbing. But he [Max] always played…

136.t: Backstage with Oscar Pettiford's USO group and J.J. Johnson
136.s: Her American fan 'Mac' took her to meet Pettiford's band; she describes the warm-up, a jam and J.J. noting she liked Bud Powell.
136.q: I had groupies, I had American groupies, and they would come … you know, this was a Japanese club so Americans are not supposed to be there. So I had these groupies, about four of them, they were in the backstage and listening. And this club, downstairs there was a coffee shop, Japanese coffee…

109.t: Back in New York; Minton's again; meeting Milt Jackson
109.s: He worked with Stan Getz, then returned to Minton's, and recalls meeting Milt Jackson, Ray Brown and Joe Harris on 52nd Street with Dizzy's big band.
109.ch: MJQ, Pettiford and the move to Paris
109.q: And I started out with -- well, I worked with Stan Getz, with Duke Jordan and Bill Crow on bass. Then I went back to Minton's.

109.t: The Milt Jackson Quartet at Minton's and Newport
109.s: The group that became the MJQ began as the Milt Jackson Quartet with Percy Heath and Horace Silver, played the first Newport festival, and swung before John Lewis's subdued style.
109.ch: MJQ, Pettiford and the move to Paris
109.q: And Bags, yeah. Yeah, that was the quartet. Then when I went to Minton's we hired Sonny Rollins. So I got -- Sonny was hanging around, not doing much.

484.t: Charlie Spivak and Frank Horne's coffee sessions
484.s: Charlie Spivak and his band visit Pensacola and gather at Frank Horne's house, where Spivak asks Brownlee about old-timers.
484.q: has his own band well he's Charlie Spivak man good thing you got a good retentive mind and a memory Charlie Spivak he was at the Rose Pelton not so long ago I think he may still be there as far as I know

485.t: Meeting Oscar Peterson and USO tour musicians
485.s: Oscar Peterson was the first great pianist she met; she recalls USO visitors like Pettiford, J.J. Johnson and Howard McGhee, and hearing J.J. warm up.
485.ch: Dance halls and learning jazz in Japan
485.q: Yes. The first great pianist I had met actually in person was Oscar Peterson. That was in 1953 I believe. That was the first time the American jazz group came to Japan for the Japanese audience. Before that a few groups came to Japan but they were for the USO

486.t: First records with Tony Scott and the Minton's gig
486.s: Katz's first records with Tony Scott and about six months at Minton's with Philly Joe Jones and Milt Hinton.
486.q: Yup. And they’re good records. The first one was done — not the very first one, the first one was at an Army camp in New Jersey with Milt and I forget who the drummer was, and Tony. We played jobs all over. But when you got this Minton’s gig, it was about now, the early part of 1953, we were there…

487.t: Joining Mongo's band and how 'Watermelon Man' reached Mongo
487.s: Donald Byrd recommends Herbie Hancock, Mongo adopts 'Watermelon Man', horn phrasing and the passed-on 'Cantaloupe Island'.
487.q: I was the one. I don’t know whether you read the story Herbie Hancock has told how it got to Mongo. Herbie had recorded “Watermelon Man” I think around the summer of ’92. And somewhere down the line Mongo was doing — oh I remember — Mongo was playing a gig in a little club in the Bronx and Chick…

488.t: Max Roach's temperament and the Beehive story with Clifford Brown
488.s: Roach was emotionally open and volatile; at the Beehive in Chicago he lowered his volume when Clifford Brown whispered to him.
488.ch: Max Roach, M'Boom and Sun Ra
488.q: Oh man, that was an education in itself. I mean here’s a person who had a variation from piano to quadruple forte, even emotionally. You know I mean he could be the most kindest, most loving person in the world, gentle. But there were times when you could

489.t: Rollins's repertoire and the audition at Fantasy
489.s: Rollins knew many tunes in several keys; Soskin's midnight audition at Fantasy with only Orrin and Sonny got him the gig alongside Tony Williams and Donald Byrd.
489.q: Yes. Well repertoire is definitely important. So I mean look, Sonny knew so many tunes, you know ridiculous. He knew so many tunes, not only knew the tunes but knew them in several keys. So I would tell people learn the tunes and learn them in several different keys. And that’s very important to do.

122.s: With the Black Hawk cutting back, he works Sundays and with Richardson's quartet at the Village in Richmond; Rowe mentions Richardson.
122.q: Well I’ve been lucky. Just blessed, blessed. Then many times I get a break. The drummers would come in. Shelly Manne, Max came in, by then I had left, I was with Fatha Hines and I went down on the jam session, or went down on the performance night to see Max. Because hell he was the man. And a…

490.t: Learning Rhythm changes and joining Max Roach's band
490.s: An older tenor player corrects how he plays I Got Rhythm; after Clifford Brown's death he joined Max Roach with Donald Byrd and Sonny Rollins for about three months.
490.ch: Early gigs, Max Roach, leaving Detroit
490.q: Ruth Brown? Very nice. You know, and then there were a lot of older musicians, who were good musicians, you know. Abe Woodley, I mean I can name names, you know. I can see faces probably more than name names, you know. Um, I can remember a cat telling me, “Barry, you need to learn how to play I Got…

491.t: How Philly Joe got his name, and the Tadd Dameron 10-inch session with Clifford Brown
491.s: Philly Joe stopped his streetcar to visit the club; Tadd Dameron renamed him Philly Joe Jones in 1953, and Golson recalls the tiny studio session with Clifford Brown close to his ear.
491.q: Philly Joe’s route came right up 11th Street, where the Down Beat Club was, on 11th Street. Philly came up one night, stopped the car in front of the Down Beat, opened the doors, got off, and went up, and took a club. Now all the people on the streetcar, they’re going crazy. He goes up into the –…

135.t: How the Milt Jackson Quartet began: the 'Milt Meets Sid' reunion date
135.s: Heath explains the quartet grew from Milt, John, Kenny and Percy and a late 1951 reunion date with Ray Brown while John studied at Manhattan School.
135.ch: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
135.q: Well, we had been playing with Milt, John, Kenny, myself. It must have been in late ’51, Ray Brown came to town and they had this record date on Dizzy’s label, I guess it was DG, and it was old reunion time for them having been that rhythm section with Dizzy’s Big Band, which spelled the trumpet…

471.t: Competitive stories: Philly Joe, Clifford Brown and Chet Baker
471.s: Cobb tells how Philly Joe and Clifford Brown came up in Philadelphia and how Dizzy sent Chet Baker to challenge Miles.
471.ch: Cannonball, Miles and the New York scene
471.q: . . . helped some of that. Dave Brubeck is probably – probably got Morello into it. So, like that. I basically listened more to Max, I think, as most drummers were then. Then was – after that was Philly Joe. Philly, I met him when I was with Earl Bostic. I think he was still in Philadelphia driving…

492.t: Booker's grief over Clifford Brown and joining Max Roach
492.s: Booker returns to Memphis in tears after Brownie's death and later joins Max Roach; Charlie Haden calls him king of the eighth notes.
492.ch: Booker Little and the Manassas circle
492.q: Anyways, when Brownie died, ’55 or ’56 he came back to Memphis. I was still ­ he came back in Christmas time and he said - he was crying. He said to me, man he said to me, “You know, Clifford’s gone.” He said, “Why couldn’t it have been me?” I don’t know young cats have that deep of a soul. He…

93.t: Fellow patients and Pickin' Joe Steele's rapid tap
93.s: Patients included Bud Powell and a saxophonist; Green recalls tap dancer Joe Steele, who developed Little Buck and Arthur Duncan, and demonstrates his rapid tap.
93.ch: Split, hospital and decline of tap
93.q: Yes. Pickin' John Steele, you know -- Bud Powell, and some gentleman from the Ted Rayburn Orchestra, an alto saxophone player -- I think he name was Ross.
